title: Vocabulary Skills: Context Clues, Word Parts, Spelling and Idioms
summary: Work out unfamiliar words from context and word parts, answer 'find a word' and technical-term questions, and master the spelling rules and British idioms that matter in Checkpoint 6.

blocks.text: Why vocabulary matters in Checkpoint 6

Vocabulary is tested in **both** papers. In **Section A Reading** (25 marks in Paper 1 Non-fiction and 25 marks in Paper 2 Fiction), you will meet questions such as 'Find **one word** that means...', 'Match each technical term to its definition', or 'What does this phrase mean?'. In **Section B Writing**, two of the five marking areas are about words: **Vocabulary and language (3 marks)** and **Word structure (spelling) (3 marks)**.
So this page teaches you two things: how to **work out** words you do not know when you read, and how to **use and spell** words correctly when you write.

rows: Reading: 'What does the word ... mean?' and 'Find a word that means...'
Reading: working out long words. Writing: spelling and building new words.
Reading: 'in your own words' answers. Writing: avoiding repeating the same word.
Reading: matching subject words (science, geography, sport) to definitions in information texts.
Writing: the 3 spelling marks in every piece you write.
Reading: understanding figurative expressions. Writing: a natural voice in stories, diaries and informal letters.

blocks.text: 1. Context clues: working out a word you don't know
A **context clue** is a hint in the words or sentences around a difficult word. Writers often help you, even in an exam. You do not need to know the word already. You need to be a detective.

rows: The meaning is given straight after the word, often after 'which means', 'or', 'that is', or between commas, dashes or brackets.
The desert fox is nocturnal (it sleeps all day and hunts at night).
A word with the same meaning is nearby.
The path was narrow. It was so thin that we walked in a line.
A word with the opposite meaning is nearby, often after 'but', 'however', 'unlike'.
Unlike his timid brother, Ziad was bold and loved trying new things.
Examples show what the word means.
We packed provisions such as bread, cheese, dates and water.
The result tells you the meaning.
The road was hazardous, so the police closed it until the ice melted.
The whole sentence or paragraph tells you.
After running for an hour, Sara was famished and ate three sandwiches.
Break the word into prefix + root + suffix.
unbreakable = un (not) + break + able (can be) = cannot be broken

blocks.text: **Signal words** tell you what kind of clue is coming:

rows: but, however, although, unlike, whereas, instead
Contrast: the word means the OPPOSITE of the clue.
so, because, as a result, therefore
such as, for example, including, like
which means, or, in other words, that is, a pair of dashes, brackets
Definition / restatement (extra information explaining the word).

blocks.title: The 4-step method for 'What does this word mean?'
items: 1. Find the word and read the **whole sentence** plus the sentences before and after.
2. Look for a clue: definition, synonym, contrast, example, cause and effect.
3. Decide if the word is positive or negative, and what word class it is (noun, verb, adjective).
4. **Replace** the word with your meaning and read the sentence again. If it makes sense, you are right.

blocks.text: **Worked mini-example.** Text: 'The kitten was so docile that it let the children carry it around all afternoon without a single scratch.' Question: What does 'docile' mean? (1 mark). **Answer:** calm and gentle / easy to handle. **Why:** cause and effect clue: because it is docile, it lets children carry it and never scratches. Test: 'The kitten was so gentle that...' makes sense.
2. 'Find a word or phrase that means...' questions
You are given a meaning and told where to look. You must copy the **exact** word or phrase from the text.

items: **Circle** the instruction: 'one word' means ONE word only. Two words, even if correct, can score zero.
**Underline** where to look: 'in paragraph 2', 'in lines 5-8'. Do not search anywhere else.
Work out the **word class** of the meaning. If the meaning is 'very tired' (adjective), the answer is an adjective (exhausted), not a verb.
Read the paragraph and test each possible word by putting the meaning in its place.
Copy the word **exactly**, with the same spelling and ending (crept, not creep).

blocks.text: **Worked mini-example.** Paragraph 2: 'At the back of the cupboard, behind old jars, Hana found a tiny wooden box. It was ancient, its paint faded and cracked.' Question: Find **one word** in paragraph 2 that means 'very old'. **Answer:** ancient. ('faded' is a trap: it describes the paint, not the age.)

blocks.title: Common traps
items: Writing a whole phrase when the question says 'one word'.
Writing your own synonym instead of copying the word from the text.
Choosing a word from the wrong paragraph.
Choosing a word with a similar topic but a different meaning (faded vs ancient).

blocks.text: 3. Matching technical terms to definitions

Information texts in Paper 1 (about science, nature, sport, history, technology) often contain **technical terms**: special words for that subject. A question can give you several terms and ask you to **match each one to its definition**, usually by drawing lines or writing letters.

**Method:** (1) Find each term in the text. (2) Read the sentence around it: the writer often explains it with a definition clue. (3) Match the terms you are **sure** of first. (4) The last one is usually the one left over, but still check it makes sense.

**Worked mini-example.** Text: 'Bees collect nectar, the sweet liquid inside flowers. As they move from flower to flower, they pollinate the plants, carrying tiny grains of pollen that help new seeds form. Back at the hive, the bees store honey in wax cells called a honeycomb.'

rows: carry pollen from one flower to another so seeds can grow
the wax cells where honey is stored

blocks.text: Notice that every definition was in the text itself: the writer explained the words using commas and 'called'. That is why reading the sentence around the term is the key step.
4. Word roots, prefixes and suffixes

Many long words are built from small parts. A **prefix** goes at the **start** and changes the meaning. A **suffix** goes at the **end** and often changes the **word class**. The **root** is the main part.

**Using word parts in a reading question.** 'The old bridge was unrepairable.' un- (not) + repair (fix) + -able (can be) = **cannot be fixed**. Even if you have never seen the word, you can explain it.

blocks.title: Spelling tip for prefixes
blocks.text: Adding a prefix never changes the spelling of the root: dis + appear = disappear (one s), dis + satisfied = dissatisfied (two s), mis + spell = misspell (two s), un + necessary = unnecessary (two n).
5. Synonyms, antonyms and shades of meaning

A **synonym** means the same or almost the same (big / large / huge). An **antonym** means the opposite (big / small). Synonyms are rarely exactly the same: they differ in **strength**. Choosing the right strength is what makes writing precise.

blocks.title: 'In your own words' questions
blocks.text: When a question says 'in your own words', you must not copy the key words from the text. Replace each key word with a synonym. Text: 'The villagers were terrified of the forest.' Own words: 'The people who lived in the village were very frightened of the woods.'
6. Spelling: the rules that save marks
Spelling is marked in **every** piece of writing under **Word structure (spelling)**, 3 marks. These rules cover most of the mistakes Year 6 students make.

rows: i before e when the sound is 'ee', except after c
Exceptions: weird, seize, protein. 'ay' sound = e before i: eight, neighbour, weigh.
Drop the silent e before a vowel suffix (-ing, -ed, -able)
make + ing = making, hope + ed = hoped, love + able = lovable
Keep the e before a consonant suffix: hopeful, movement, lovely.
Consonant + y: change y to i
happy + ness = happiness, carry + ed = carried, baby → babies
Keep y before -ing: carrying, studying. Vowel + y: just add (played, enjoys).
Double the last consonant (short vowel + one consonant) before a vowel suffix
stop → stopping, swim → swimmer, begin → beginning, big → biggest
No doubling when there are two vowels or two consonants: rain → raining, jump → jumped.
Add -es after s, sh, ch, x, z
leaf → leaves, knife → knives, half → halves
'full' on its own has two l's.
-able when the root is a whole word, -ible when it is not
Check in a dictionary when unsure.
British spelling doubles l before a vowel suffix
travel → travelled, cancel → cancelled, label → labelled

blocks.text: **Homophones** sound the same but are spelt differently. A spell-checker cannot catch them, so learn them well.

rows: a place (here, there) / belongs to them / they are
belongs to it / it is (it's always = it is or it has)
towards / also or too much / the number 2
place / past of 'are' / put on clothes
stop a car / smash or a rest
a piece of pie / peace = no war
British: practice is the noun, practise is the verb (I practise every day at football practice).

blocks.text: **Commonly misspelt words: learn these by heart.**

blocks.title: كيف تحصل على 3/3 في الإملاء؟
items: احفظ الكلمات التي يخطئ فيها الطلاب كثيرًا (because / friend / beautiful / definitely) واكتبها صحيحة في كل مرة.
استخدم الإملاء البريطاني دائمًا: colour وليس color، و favourite وليس favorite.
انتبه للكلمات المتشابهة في النطق: their / there / they're و your / you're.
في آخر 3 أو 4 دقائق من الكتابة: راجع الإملاء كلمة كلمة، خاصة الكلمات الطويلة.

blocks.text: 7. Idioms (common British idioms)

An **idiom** is a fixed expression whose meaning is **different** from the meaning of each word. 'It's raining cats and dogs' has nothing to do with animals: it means it is raining very heavily. In reading, use the context to work out the meaning. In writing, one well-chosen idiom in a story's dialogue, a diary or an informal letter adds a natural voice. Do not use idioms in formal reports.

rows: The spelling test was a piece of cake.
make people feel relaxed when they first meet
Omar told a joke to break the ice on the first day.
I stayed home because I was under the weather.
My cousin visits once in a blue moon.
With exams next week, it's time to hit the books.
Yara was over the moon with her result.
let the cat out of the bag
Ali let the cat out of the bag about the surprise party.
cost an arm and a leg
That bike costs an arm and a leg.
The park is a stone's throw from my house.
He was on cloud nine after scoring the winning goal.
Karim was in hot water for forgetting his homework.
I had butterflies in my stomach before the show.
Can you keep an eye on my bag?
We're tired, so let's call it a day.
bite off more than you can chew
Joining four clubs was biting off more than I could chew.
by the skin of your teeth
We caught the train by the skin of our teeth.
what you do matters more than what you say
Don't just promise to help. Actions speak louder than words.
it is better to do something late than not at all
You finished the project? Better late than never!
something bad that turns out good
Missing the bus was a blessing in disguise: I met an old friend.
Tell me the story. I'm all ears!
nervous and unsure before doing something
She got cold feet before the competition.
After the argument, he gave me the cold shoulder.
These pencils were cheap as chips.
a lazy person who watches a lot of TV
Don't be a couch potato. Come for a walk!
My brother and I don't always see eye to eye.
Relax, I'm only pulling your leg.
His costume was a bit over the top.
The goalkeeper was really on the ball today.

blocks.title: How to answer an idiom question
blocks.text: Never explain the words literally. Ask: what is happening in the story at this moment? 'When Adam saw the mess, he hit the roof.' Adam is clearly not climbing anything: from the context (a mess), 'hit the roof' must mean he became very angry.
8. Strong words to use in your own writing
To reach 3/3 in **Vocabulary and language**, choose words that are precise and match the mood and text type. Here are useful upgrades.

items: exhausted
very tired (instead of 'very tired')
furious
very angry
delighted
very pleased
terrified
very frightened
enormous / gigantic
very big
ancient
very old
gleaming
shining brightly (clean, polished things)
glimpse
see something for a moment
stumble
almost fall while walking
whisper / mutter
speak quietly / speak quietly and crossly
dash / sprint
run very fast
peer
look closely at something hard to see
essential
absolutely necessary (good for persuasive and information writing)
benefit
a good result or advantage (non-fiction)
determined
not giving up

blocks.text: Common mistakes

items: Giving more than one word when the question says 'one word'.
Using your own word in 'find a word' questions instead of copying from the text.
Copying the text in 'own words' questions.
Explaining an idiom literally.
Using American spelling (color, favorite) in a British exam.
Writing 'carefull', 'beautifull' (the suffix -ful has one l).
Mixing up there/their/they're and its/it's.

blocks.title: أسئلة Find a word: انتبه للتعليمات
items: إذا قال السؤال one word، فاكتب كلمة واحدة فقط. حتى لو كتبت كلمتين صحيحتين ستحصل على صفر.
انقل الكلمة من النص كما هي تمامًا، ومن الفقرة التي حددها السؤال.
إذا قال السؤال in your own words، فلا تنقل من النص، بل استخدم مرادفات.

blocks.text: Checklist

items: I can use 7 types of context clue and the signal words.
I always check 'one word' or 'phrase', and which paragraph.
I can match technical terms using the sentence around them.
I know the main prefixes, suffixes and roots.
I choose synonyms with the right strength.
I know the spelling rules, homophones and British spellings.
I can work out an idiom from the context.

blocks.text: Practice questions
All texts are short and original. Try each one before opening the answer.

items.q: 'The cave was so dim that we could hardly see our own hands.' What does 'dim' mean? (1 mark)
items.a: dark / not bright. Cause and effect clue: we could hardly see our hands.

items.q: 'Unlike the noisy city, the village was tranquil.' What does 'tranquil' mean? Which clue helped you? (2 marks)
items.a: calm / quiet / peaceful (1). Contrast clue: 'Unlike' tells us it is the opposite of 'noisy' (1).

items.q: 'Camels can survive in arid places – areas that get almost no rain – where most animals would die.' What does 'arid' mean? (1 mark)
items.a: very dry. Definition clue: the pair of dashes adds extra information explaining the word.

items.q: Paragraph: 'The explorers were weary after climbing all day. Their legs ached and they could barely keep their eyes open.' Find ONE word that means 'very tired'. (1 mark)
items.a: weary

items.q: Paragraph: 'The vast desert stretched in every direction. There was nothing but sand for hundreds of kilometres.' Find ONE word that means 'very large'. (1 mark)
items.a: vast

items.q: Match each term to its meaning. Text: 'Volcanoes form where hot, melted rock called magma rises from deep underground. When it bursts out of the volcano, the rock is called lava. The explosion itself is an eruption. The opening at the top is the crater.' Terms: magma, lava, eruption, crater. (2 marks)
items.a: magma = melted rock underground / lava = melted rock that has come out of the volcano / eruption = when the volcano explodes / bursts out / crater = the opening at the top of the volcano. (4 correct = 2 marks, 2-3 correct = 1 mark.)

items.q: What does 'misjudge' mean? Use the prefix to explain. (1 mark)
items.a: To judge wrongly. The prefix 'mis-' means wrongly.

items.q: Add a prefix to make the opposite: (a) possible (b) legal (c) honest (d) regular (2 marks)
items.a: (a) impossible (b) illegal (c) dishonest (d) irregular.

items.q: Change the word into a noun using a suffix: (a) kind (b) enjoy (c) decide (d) dark (2 marks)
items.a: (a) kindness (b) enjoyment (c) decision (d) darkness.

items.q: Explain the meaning of 'telescope' using its parts. (1 mark)
items.a: tele (far) + scope (look) = an instrument for looking at things that are far away.

items.q: Put in order from weakest to strongest: furious, annoyed, angry. (1 mark)
items.a: annoyed, angry, furious.

items.q: Give an antonym for each: (a) ancient (b) generous (c) arrive (d) victory (2 marks)
items.a: (a) modern / new (b) selfish / mean (c) depart / leave (d) defeat.

items.q: In your own words, explain: 'The children were astonished by the enormous whale.' (2 marks)
items.a: Example: The young people were very surprised by the huge whale. ('astonished' replaced by 'very surprised', 'enormous' by 'huge'. 1 mark for each key word changed correctly.)

items.q: Correct the spelling: (a) hopeing (b) carryed (c) stoped (d) beautifull (2 marks)
items.a: (a) hoping (drop the e) (b) carried (y to i) (c) stopped (double the consonant) (d) beautiful (-ful has one l).

items.q: Choose the correct word: (a) The dog wagged (its / it's) tail. (b) (Their / There / They're) going to the beach. (c) I need to (practice / practise) my lines. (2 marks)
items.a: (a) its (b) They're (c) practise (British verb).

items.q: Write the British spelling: color, center, organize, traveled. (2 marks)
items.a: colour, centre, organise, travelled.

items.q: 'When Sami heard he had won the trip, he was over the moon.' What does the idiom mean? (1 mark)
items.a: He was extremely happy.

items.q: 'Laila had butterflies in her stomach as she walked on stage.' What does this tell us about Laila? (1 mark)
items.a: She felt very nervous.

items.q: 'Don't let the cat out of the bag about Mum's present!' What is the speaker asking? (1 mark)
items.a: Not to tell the secret about the present by mistake.

items.q: Which idiom means 'very rarely'? A) a piece of cake B) once in a blue moon C) on the ball D) cold feet (1 mark)
items.a: B) once in a blue moon.
